questions: Why must the force point at the centre rather than along the direction of motion?
If the centre-seeking force suddenly vanished, what path would the satellite take?
segments.say: Circular motion needs a centre-seeking push. A satellite stays on its circular path only because something keeps pulling it towards the centre. Watch the force arrow swing round the orbit: at the right, at the top, at the left, it always points at the planet in the middle. No centre-seeking push, no circle - the satellite would leave on a tangent. Keep your student notes open at the centripetal force definition for this scene.

questions: A car doubles its speed on the same bend. By what factor does the friction needed grow?
Why does doubling the radius halve the force at the same speed?
segments.say: How big is the centre-seeking force. The acceleration is a = v^2/r and the force is F = mv^2/r. Watch the readout: double the speed and the force goes 1 to 4, then double the radius and it falls 4 to 2. The v-squared is the scaling to fear in every exam question. Now try the first computation on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: What plays the role of the string tension for the Moon?
If the Moon were twice as far away, how would the gravitational force on it change?
segments.say: Gravity holds the Moon in orbit. For the Moon there is no string and no friction: gravity itself, F = GMm/r^2, is the centripetal force. Set the two formulas equal and the orbital speed follows. Every orbit is a fall that keeps missing the Earth. Compare the gravitation definition in your student notes before we sync an orbit.

questions: Why is a 24-hour period alone not enough for a satellite to hover over one spot?
What angular speed must a geostationary satellite have, compared with the Earth?
segments.say: Geostationary orbits hover over one spot. Period exactly 24 hours, above the equator, west to east with the Earth below: the synced satellite hangs over its home point while the drifter falls behind. Weather and broadcast satellites live here. Check the period definition in your student notes, then look ahead to the exit ticket question on this scene.

questions: In one sentence, what force acts outward on a passenger in a sharp turn?
How would you correct a classmate who insists a centrifugal force flung them into the door?
segments.say: Misconception: the fling-off force. The animation boxes the wrong idea, draws the imagined outward arrow, then removes both: your body keeps going straight on the tangent while the seat pushes you inward. Finish the worksheet trap question now, then the exit ticket on your own - the last question revisits exactly this scene.
segments.watchFor: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. Listen and look for it on the worksheet and in pair talk: any answer inventing an outward force shows the trap reading, not the inertia reading - send them back to the tangent line the body actually follows.
